stories.headline: The Last Citizen
stories.title: The Last Citizen
stories.summary: The morning train from Katra reaches Srinagar a little after eleven. On the platform at Nowgam last week I watched a grandmother from Kupwara step down from it, having crossed the Chenab on a bridge higher than the Eiffel Tower, sitting, with a cup of tea, in three hours. For most of my life "I took the train to Srinagar" was a sentence nobody in the Valley could say. The line was sanctioned in 1994. Every government since owned a piece of it. This one finished it. On 7 October 2001, in Gandhinagar, a man who had never sat in a legislature took oath as Chief Minister of a state nine months out from an earthquake that had killed fourteen thousand people. Twenty-five years later he is Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, and there has not been one day in that quarter century when he was not the elected head of a government. No Indian, not Jyoti Basu, not Pawan Chamling, has been continuously answerable to voters for so long. The anniversary invites praise, and praise is the one thing he has never shown any sign of needing. It deserves instead an argument that can be tested. Here is mine. These twenty-five years are the story of the Indian state learning to reach its last citizen, first in one state and then in all of them. What travelled from Gandhinagar to Delhi was a method, not a mood: saturation targets instead of coverage ratios, technology used as an equaliser, several schemes converging on one household, deadlines reviewed in person. It is the method, more than the man, that explains the numbers. And the numbers that settle the argument are not the government's own; they are the Census, the Registrar General's and the World Bank's. Remember the country of 2001. Fifty-six households in a hundred had electricity, thirty-six a latrine, thirty-seven a tap, eighteen a gas connection. One child in fifteen died before its first birthday. A bank account was a favour, and a gas cylinder came with a politician's letter. That was the baseline. Then Gujarat. In 2003 the state separated the farm feeder from the village feeder and gave the village twenty-four-hour power; agricultural output grew at 9.6 percent a year between 2000 and 2007, by IFPRI's count, against 2.9 percent for India. The Soil Health Card was a Gujarat card before it was an Indian one. The grievance screen in the Chief Minister's office became PRAGATI. The Garib Kalyan Mela became the saturation camp every state now runs. Gujarat was the laboratory. India was the canvas. On the canvas, the household became the unit of delivery. Jan Dhan, mocked as a zero-balance gesture in 2014, holds 59 crore accounts today, more than half of them women's, and they are the rails on which every later transfer ran. A woman who has sat in those kitchens counts the cylinder in hours returned, not in connections. Ujjwala put 10.57 crore cylinders into kitchens that had cooked on wood. Rural households with a tap went from 3.23 crore in 2019 to 15.85 crore. Ayushman Bharat has paid for 13.25 crore hospital admissions. Direct transfer has removed 3.48 lakh crore rupees of leakage. The national highway network grew from 91,287 kilometres to 1,46,572; airports from 74 to 165; UPI, which did not exist in 2014, moved 314 lakh crore rupees last year. Infant mortality fell from 39 to 24 per thousand. Three crore rural women have crossed the Lakhpati Didi line. Left-wing extremism, which touched 126 districts in 2013, is confined to eleven. NITI Aayog's poverty index fell from 29 percent to 11, which is 24.82 crore people; the World Bank's three-dollar line fell from 27 percent to just over five. Neither figure is the government's own. What was the method's hardest test? I can answer that, because I live inside it. In 2001 Jammu and Kashmir recorded 4,522 terrorist incidents and 996 civilians killed. In 2025 it recorded 35 incidents and 92 deaths in all, the least violent year in more than two decades. Local recruitment into militancy, 125 young men in 2021, was seven in 2024. Stone-pelting has gone. The G20 met in Srinagar in May 2023. Since 2019, 34,260 people have been elected to panchayats and councils in a territory that for decades had almost none, and 7.85 crore visitors came to the Union Territory in the three years to 2025, against 4.76 crore in the three years to 2018, even though the Valley's own arrivals halved in 2025 after Pahalgam. The men who send killers across the Line retain the capacity: twenty-six civilians were murdered at Pahalgam in April 2025, and the answer, Operation Sindoor, came on 7 May. Normalcy here is a trend that has to be defended every year, not a settled fact. But the trend is real, and a Kashmiri who denies it forfeits the right to be believed on the rest. The rest is this. In August 2019 the Valley's communications were restricted, the internet did not fully return for eighteen months, and the leaders of the mainstream parties, three former Chief Ministers among them, were placed in preventive detention. Those were hard months, and I do not write around them. They were also the reason a change that every earlier turn in this Valley had paid for in blood passed without it. Elections followed as the Supreme Court directed; turnout was 64 percent; an elected government took office in October 2024. Statehood has not yet been restored. The Prime Minister and the Home Minister have given their word that it will be, at the appropriate time, and the Court asked for it at the earliest in December 2023. When the Assembly voted on 28 September, my party objected to a resolution that reached back to the position before 2019, not to statehood itself. I belong to the party that gave the word, and I have no doubt it will be kept; the security data in this essay is the case that the time is approaching. When it comes, let it come with the Pandits' return built into it, with houses and not only posts, and with the jobs that keep young men on the platform and off the hill. Nor should the national ledger be read without its debit side, and a member of the governing party should be the first to read it. Four crore rural households still wait for a tap, and the mission that reached 15.85 crore will be judged on the last four, which are the hardest. The labour survey still finds a quarter of the young in neither work nor training, and no government should be comfortable with that. Manipur tested the state's reach harder than anywhere else, and the peace there is still being rebuilt. The second wave of 2021 found the one shortage, oxygen, that nobody had been counting, and the state learned to count it. Demonetisation is still argued over; what nobody argues about is the digital habit it built, which became UPI. By the IMF's own tables India is third in purchasing power, within a few hundred billion dollars of fourth place in current dollars, and growing faster than every economy above it. An argument that cannot survive its objections is not an argument. This one does, because not one of them is an objection to reach, scale or speed. So what will outlast him? The rails: identity, account, payment, which no successor can switch off. The direct transfer, which made the intermediary politically expendable. The GST Council, in which the Centre holds one vote in three and almost every decision has been taken by consensus. The doctrine that an attack is answered across the Line. The three criminal codes of 2024, and a temple at Ayodhya built after a unanimous Supreme Court judgment, which are the same confidence turned inward. And one thing larger than all of these: Indians now expect their state to arrive. In 2001 a tap was a favour. In 2026 its absence is a grievance that a Collector in Nuh expects to be ranked on. That change in expectation is the structural achievement, and a people who have learned to expect delivery do not unlearn it when the deliverer changes. What must now be built into the state is the dashboard itself, so that the deadline holds when the review passes to other hands. The Prime Minister has said that the goal is a developed India by 2047, and that no one man is the goal. The next decade will show whether the method has been made the state's own, as he intends. The afternoon train leaves Srinagar at two. I went back to watch it go: students for Jammu, pilgrims, a box of apples wrapped in newspaper, a soldier asleep before the platform had cleared. The state learned, over a quarter century, to arrive. It has not yet learned to stay. That is the work of the next twenty-five years, and it belongs to everyone who will still be here when the man who taught it to arrive is not. The train is pulling out. The platform is ours. (The Author is Vice President, Bharatiya Janata Party, Jammu and Kashmir. She can be reached at: sganai19@gmail.com)

stories.headline: Mehbooba’s condemnation without PDP’s participation under scrutiny
stories.title: Mehbooba’s condemnation without PDP’s participation under scrutiny
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: People’s Democratic Party (PDP) President and former chief minister Mehbooba Mufti on Saturday drew parallels between restrictions imposed in New Delhi during protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the communication blackout and security clampdown in Kashmir following the abrogation of Article 370. However, the absence of PDP leaders from the opposition’s street mobilisation in Delhi has raised questions about the party’s political positioning and its willingness to participate in a coordinated opposition campaign against the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government. Criticising the restriction on ‘X’, Mehbooba posted: “Today’s Delhi is a chilling reminder of Kashmir after the unconstitutional abrogation of Article 370. People were locked in their homes, the internet was shut down, and an entire region was placed under siege. The BJP then brazenly claimed that nobody had protested. Today, with Delhi under siege, trains halted, and roads to Jantar Mantar sealed, they may repeat the same lie, claiming that nobody protested against Gyanesh Kumar. First crush the protest, then deny it ever happened. This is how enforced silence is passed off as consent.” While her words echoed the concerns articulated by most opposition leaders, the party’s visible participation in the protests has remained conspicuously limited. The political messaging has raised a question that the PDP has yet to answer publicly. If the restrictions in Delhi evoke such strong comparisons with Kashmir, why has that outrage not translated into PDP leaders’ visible presence at the protests? Talking to Greater Kashmir, PDP chief spokesperson Mehbooba Beg said, “In principle, every sensible citizen protests this naked onslaught of democracy. The institution of the Election Commission of India has got into disrepute. Registering protest is important, whether one does it through tweets, statements, or hits the streets.” He said that the Delhi protests are genuine as the ‘vote theft’ affects the 13.5 crore people including the women of West Bengal, the minorities, and the citizens of the entire country. The senior PDP leader said that the CEC Gyanesh Kumar should tender his resignation as he headed an institution that was once led by an honest person like T N Seshan. “CEC Gyanesh Kumar brought such an institution into disrepute and for that history will not judge him kindly,” he said. “The Indian Express’ investigation illustrated that anti-BJP voters had been deleted across the country and the protest is important as there was a small winning margin on many seats. Furthermore, the stand taken by the other two Election Commissioners has also made the issue of ‘vote theft’ clear.” Beg said that PDP’s stand against New Delhi had been clear after August 2019. “It was for the consistent stand taken by the PDP that the PDP chief Mehbooba Mufti’s mother (Gulshan Nazir) had been grilled by the Enforcement Directorate,” he said. While Mehbooba took to microblogging site ‘X’ on Saturday, all senior PDP leaders and legislators – Waheed-ur-Rehman Para, Muhammad Fayaz Mir, and Rafiq Ahmad Naik - as well as Mehbooba’s daughter, Iltija Mufti, were conspicuous by their absence from the Delhi mobilisation. Talking to Greater Kashmir, MLA Kupwara Muhammad Fayaz Mir and MLA Tral Rafiq Ahmad Naik said that no directions had been issued to them for participating in the Delhi protests. “I’m in Kupwara and, so far, I haven’t received any such direction,” Mir said. Naik said that he was the party’s foot soldier and would do whatever was asked of him by the party high command. Their participation could have lent greater weight to the PDP’s condemnation of the restrictions and demonstrated that its opposition extended beyond statements and social media posts. PDP’s non-participation in Delhi mobilisation leaves the party open to questions about the consistency of its opposition and the extent to which it is prepared to join a campaign beyond its own political platforms. PDP has continued to criticise the BJP-led Centre over the loss of J&K’s special status, restrictions on political activity, and other questions of civil liberties. While Mehbooba’s latest remarks reinforce the PDP’s confrontational public posture towards the Centre, the party’s absence from the Delhi protests raises questions about whether it is seeking to avoid antagonising Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) government while keeping its options open with the Congress and the wider INDIA bloc. The political metaphor of “running with the hare and hunting with the hounds” captures the suspicion surrounding this approach, as it has been denouncing the Centre’s actions but is avoiding an unambiguous demonstration of solidarity with those challenging it on the streets. PDP cannot entirely avoid scrutiny by invoking those complexities. If it believes the restrictions represent an assault on democratic freedoms, PDP leaders must explain whether they consider participation in a common opposition campaign necessary, and if not, why. Silence on that question risks allowing its opponents to portray the party’s position as selective. For Mehbooba, the immediate challenge is to reconcile the force of her public condemnation with the absence of her party’s prominent faces from the streets. The PDP’s statement may have strengthened the opposition’s argument about the curtailment of dissent. However, its absence has opened a different debate – one about whether the PDP is prepared to match its rhetoric with participation. Until the party clarifies that position, the contrast between Mehbooba’s words and her party’s political presence is likely to remain a source of scrutiny for the PDP.

stories.headline: BJP stages protest outside Congress office in Jammu
stories.title: BJP stages protest outside Congress office in Jammu
stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 10: Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday held a protest demonstration outside the Congress office in Jammu, accusing the Leader of Opposition (LoP) in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and his other party colleagues of resorting to double standards. Led by J&K BJP vice presidents Priya Sethi (former minister) and Rekha Mahajan; general secretary Sanjita Dogra; Mahila Morcha president Neha Mahajan and other senior leaders, the protesters declared that India would not tolerate the insult or humiliation of women. J&K BJP president and Rajya Sabha MP Sat Sharma was prominent among those present. J&K BJP general secretaries Baldev Singh Billawaria and Gopal Mahajan, MLAs Dr Narinder Singh, CP Ganga, Dr Devinder Manyal, Vikram Randhawa, Prof Gharu Ram, Yudhvir Sethi, Arvind Gupta, Surinder Bhagat and Rajiv Bhagat, state office bearers, Morcha Presidents and other senior leaders were also present. Raising slogans against Congress, the demonstrators criticised the Congress leadership for, what they alleged, “practising double standards on women's dignity while using slogans such as “smashing the patriarchy” to mislead the public.” The protesters demanded Rahul Gandhi's resignation, holding him accountable for the conduct and politics of his party. Sat Sharma, addressing the demonstrators, said that Rahul Gandhi should resign, take responsibility for the conduct of his party and stop preaching about women's empowerment while serious questions were being raised about the behaviour of Congress leaders towards women. He asserted that the dignity of women could not be compromised for political convenience and that those who lectured the nation on women's rights must first demonstrate consistency through their own conduct. Sat Sharma criticised Rahul Gandhi and the Congress leadership alleging that their public claims of standing for women's rights contradicted the conduct attributed to Congress leaders. He said that allegations of misbehaviour towards female police personnel by Congress leaders and workers demanded serious accountability. He further accused Congress of pursuing a political agenda targetting national security agencies and undermining public confidence in constitutional institutions. Questioning Congress's silence over serious allegations against one of its MPs in a molestation case, Sat Sharma asked why Rahul Gandhi and other senior Congress leaders had not shown the same vocal concern for women's dignity in that matter. He stressed that women's respect was not a political slogan but a fundamental social responsibility and Rahul Gandhi must answer for his party's double standards and resign rather than evade accountability. Priya Sethi said that women's dignity must remain above partisan politics and that Congress must answer for the contradiction between its public messaging and the conduct it is accused of defending. Rekha Mahajan said that women deserved respect, security and equal dignity in every sphere of life, adding that political slogans could not substitute for accountability. Sanjita Dogra said that women expected sincerity and consistency from political leaders, not selective outrage on issues concerning their rights. Neha Mahajan said that BJP's women workers would continue to raise their voices against every instance of disrespect towards women and demand accountability from those holding public office.

Led by J&K BJP vice presidents Priya Sethi (former minister) and Rekha Mahajan; general secretary Sanjita Dogra; Mahila Morcha president Neha Mahajan and other senior leaders, the protesters declared that India would not tolerate the insult or humiliation of women.
body: J&K BJP president and Rajya Sabha MP Sat Sharma was prominent among those present.

J&K BJP general secretaries Baldev Singh Billawaria and Gopal Mahajan, MLAs Dr Narinder Singh, CP Ganga, Dr Devinder Manyal, Vikram Randhawa, Prof Gharu Ram, Yudhvir Sethi, Arvind Gupta, Surinder Bhagat and Rajiv Bhagat, state office bearers, Morcha Presidents and other senior leaders were also present.

Raising slogans against Congress, the demonstrators criticised the Congress leadership for, what they alleged, “practising double standards on women's dignity while using slogans such as “smashing the patriarchy” to mislead the public.” The protesters demanded Rahul Gandhi's resignation, holding him accountable for the conduct and politics of his party.

Sat Sharma, addressing the demonstrators, said that Rahul Gandhi should resign, take responsibility for the conduct of his party and stop preaching about women's empowerment while serious questions were being raised about the behaviour of Congress leaders towards women.

He asserted that the dignity of women could not be compromised for political convenience and that those who lectured the nation on women's rights must first demonstrate consistency through their own conduct.
Sat Sharma criticised Rahul Gandhi and the Congress leadership alleging that their public claims of standing for women's rights contradicted the conduct attributed to Congress leaders.
He said that allegations of misbehaviour towards female police personnel by Congress leaders and workers demanded serious accountability.
He further accused Congress of pursuing a political agenda targetting national security agencies and undermining public confidence in constitutional institutions.

Questioning Congress's silence over serious allegations against one of its MPs in a molestation case, Sat Sharma asked why Rahul Gandhi and other senior Congress leaders had not shown the same vocal concern for women's dignity in that matter.

He stressed that women's respect was not a political slogan but a fundamental social responsibility and Rahul Gandhi must answer for his party's double standards and resign rather than evade accountability.
Priya Sethi said that women's dignity must remain above partisan politics and that Congress must answer for the contradiction between its public messaging and the conduct it is accused of defending.
Rekha Mahajan said that women deserved respect, security and equal dignity in every sphere of life, adding that political slogans could not substitute for accountability.
Sanjita Dogra said that women expected sincerity and consistency from political leaders, not selective outrage on issues concerning their rights.
Neha Mahajan said that BJP's women workers would continue to raise their voices against every instance of disrespect towards women and demand accountability from those holding public office.
